newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - London Clubs launches Capital bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - London Clubs launches Capital bid.

text.p: British casino operator London Clubs International Plc International launched a 181 million pounds ($293.2 million) offer for Capital Corporation Plc on Monday in a bid to get more gambling tables in Britain's tightly regulated industry.
But Capital Corporation rejected the bid in a statement which said it was both unwelcome and undervalued the company.
London Clubs is offering 47 new shares for every 100 Capital shares in its all-paper bid.
"The combined entity will be well positioned to develop in a way that Capital Corporation as a stand alone company cannot," Alan Goodenough, London International's chief executive said.
"I will be surprised if they do not accept it," he told Reuters before Capital's rejection statement.
London Clubs currently has seven casinos in the capital and also operates three in Egypt, one in the south of France and few on cruise ships.
Capital Corporation owns and operates two casinos in the upmarket Mayfair area of London, its Crockfords casino has 18 tables and its Colony Club has 20.

London Clubs' offer comes barely six weeks after Capital Corporation issued a profit warning for 1996 saying it would be hit by costs of 2.5 million pounds arising from the temporary closure of its Colony Club.
Capital Corp is due to announce is results on March 4, 1997. Its shares, which have weakened since the profit warning, rose 15p on Monday to close at 186-1/2.
Capital estimated that its pretax profits for 1996 would be between 8.5 million pounds and nine million pounds.
Capital's shares are currently trading on a price earnings ratio in the range of 28.8 to 30.5 times its estimated December 1996 earnings.
London Clubs' offer represents a multiple of between 30.5 and 32.2 times Capital's estimated earnings.
London Clubs' share price shed seven pence to 378.
Goodenough said the merger of the two firms would give it a better chance of winning tenders overseas especially in Europe and west Asia where the gaming industry is gradually being deregulated.
"We are looking at new markets specially in Belgium, Cyprus and South Africa," he said.
He said the merger would help London Clubs to increase the number of its tables which under present licensing restrictions in Britain was still difficult.
There are 117 licensed casinos in Britain and their operators are seeking to lift a number of regulations including a ban on use of credit cards by their customers.
Also, a gambler must currently wait 48 hours between visiting a casino and filling out a membership application and being allowed to play the tables. The industry wants to cut this to 24 hours.
The British government has already proposed some measures to deregulate the industry, including liberalisation of strict rules governing advertising.
Gambling rules are also being gradually liberalised in north America, Europe and the Middle East, where Goodenough said London Clubs would be expanding in future years.
He said the acquisition of Capital Corp, prior to reorganisation costs, would not dilute London Clubs' earnings per share in the year to March 1998 below current market expectations.
--London Newsroom 44 171 542 7717 ($ = 0.617 British Pounds)
